title: The Almost-All Theorem for Restricted Goldbach Sums Modulo a Power of Two
content: For \( q \ge 1 \) and $\gcd(a,q)=1$ we study the restricted weighted Goldbach sum $R_{a,q}(N) :=2\sum_{\substack{p_1+p_2=N,\,p_1\equiv a\pmod q}}(\log p_1)(\log p_2)$ for even $N$, with candidate main term $M_{a,q}(N) :=2C_2\varphi(q)^{-1}S(N)N$, where $C_2$ is the twin-prime constant and \( S(N) \) is the odd part of the Hardy--Littlewood singular series. We first prove an elementary local-obstruction theorem: if $q$ has an odd prime factor $\ell$, then $R_{a,q}(N)=O_q(\log N)$ on a positive-density set of even $N$, so no asymptotic of size $N/\varphi(q)$ can hold uniformly for such $q$; the restriction to $q=2^k$ used throughout the rest of the paper is therefore forced by the truth of the statement, not by convenience. For $q=2^k$ we give a fully self-contained, elementary derivation of an explicit pointwise minor-arc bound for $S_X(\alpha)$ (via Vaughan's identity with the balanced parameters $U=V=X^{2/5}$), from which we deduce an unconditional master second-moment bound \[ \sum_{N\le X}|E(N)|^2\le \frac{G}{2\varphi(q)}\frac{X^3}{\log X}(1+o(1)), \] with $G$ the Gallagher--Goldston constant. From this we prove a qualitative almost-all theorem, $\#\{N\le X\text{ even}:R_{a,q}(N)=0\}=o_q(X)$, and its effective refinement with an explicit threshold that grows like \( (\log X)^{(5+A)/2} \); we further prove that this growth is necessary, in the sense that no threshold constant independent of $X$ can achieve the same exceptional-set decay once the second moment is genuinely of order $X^3/\log X$. Finally, via the explicit formula and McCurley's zero-free region we give a sub-exponential exceptional-set bound $\#\mathcal{E}_{a,q}(X)\ll_q X\exp(-\sqrt{\log X}/R_{\mathrm{McC}})$, and show that a single real (Siegel) zero cannot invalidate it, since its contribution to the main term is itself \( o(N) \). Every result in this paper is unconditional; no Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, Density Hypothesis, or other unproved conjecture is used anywhere. We close by stating precisely why the results proved here do not, by themselves, upgrade ''almost all'' to ''all,'' and record this gap as an open question.
